title: Pauri 20, sound: bhareeai hath
tomorrow: Pauri 20, meaning: what washes the mind

lines: FROM THE UNIVERSE TO THE SINK.
cards: Muddy hands after gardening. Sticky hands after a mango. The feeling after a long day when your whole body just wants a shower.
For four stanzas, Japji has been looking up and out: countless worlds, countless names, a bull holding up the earth. Now, suddenly, it looks down at your hands.
It's about as ordinary as a picture gets, and Guru Nanak starts a new stanza with it. From the edge of the universe to the kitchen sink, in one breath.

teach.b: Here's the first line of Pauri 20 in the original: bhareeai hath pair tan deh. Word by word. Bhareeai, said BHA-ree-ai: when it's filled, when it's covered, when it's soiled.
It's built on the everyday verb for filling, as you'd fill a glass; here it means covered in dirt. Hath: hands. Pair: feet.
Tan and deh: two words for the body, one after the other, as if to say the whole body, all of it. So: when the hands, the feet, the whole body are covered in dirt. Hear the rhythm.
Bhareeai, a long rolling word, then four short ones, hath, pair, tan, deh, like four quick splashes.

teach.h: WATER, AND THE DUST COMES OFF.
teach.b: The next line, in paraphrase, gives the answer everyone knows: pour on water, and the dust comes off. Nothing mysterious. Anyone who's ever washed their hands knows it.
That's how the stanza begins, with something so obvious it almost doesn't need saying. And that's the teacher's trick.
Start with what everybody already agrees on: hands get dirty; water cleans them. Then, once you're nodding, move to something you might not have thought about.
Tomorrow we follow the stanza from the body to the mind, and see what it says washes that. Today, just the sound and the picture.

how: Pauri 20 is recited in the morning Japji Sahib; the Sikh code of conduct describes rising early, bathing, and then reciting Japji, so its opening picture of washing sits close to the morning itself.

o: the body, all of it, head to toe
the feet that carry you around

games.q: the sound of Pauri 20 — tap the pairs.

s: it opens with dirty hands, feet and body: the most ordinary picture.
the next line says water washes the dust away
nothing mysterious; everyone already knows it.
tan and deh are two words for the body
said one after the other, as if to say the whole body.

games.q: you're a teacher about to say something surprising. how does Pauri 20 begin?
o: with the surprising part, right away.
with something everyone already agrees on: water washes dirty hands.
games.why: bhareeai hath pair tan deh: start with the obvious, then, once the listener is nodding, move to the mind.

practice: Say the first line aloud once slowly, bhareeai hath pair tan deh, then again, bringing your attention to each part as you name it: hands, feet, the whole body.
Then rest your hands in your lap, palms up, and simply feel them: warm or cool, heavy or light.

wordCard.voice: Deh. The body: named alongside tan in this pauri's opening, bhareeai hath pair tan deh, when hands, feet and body are soiled, and water washes the dust away.

orig.note: Gurmukhi, Japji Pauri 20, line 1: when hands, feet and body are soiled.

carryVoice: Your line: bhareeai hath. The body comes first in this stanza; the mind comes next. See you tomorrow.
